claim: Simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs) comprise a large group of primate lentiviruses that endemically infect African monkeys.
source: Simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs) comprise a large group of primate lentiviruses that endemically infect African monkeys.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HIV-1 spilled over to humans from the SIV viral reservoir, but not directly from monkeys to humans.
source: HIV-1 spilled over to humans from this viral reservoir, but the spillover did not occur directly from monkeys to humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A key event in HIV-1 emergence was the introduction of SIVs into great apes, which set the stage for infection of humans.
source: Instead, a key event was the introduction of SIVs into great apes, which then set the stage for infection of humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ancestral CD4 at the hominin and hominid nodes fully supported entry of diverse SIV isolates related to viruses that initially jumped to apes.
source: These ancestral CD4s fully supported entry of diverse SIV isolates related to the viruses that made this initial jump to apes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E, where ancestral CD4s were tested for viral entry.

claim: Modern chimpanzee and gorilla CD4 orthologs are more resistant to SIV entry than ancestral CD4s.
source: In stark contrast, modern chimpanzee and gorilla CD4 orthologs are more resistant to these viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E comparing modern and ancestral CD4s.

claim: CD4 gene sequences from 32 gorilla individuals of two species encode 8 unique CD4 protein variants.
source: We acquired CD4 gene sequences from 32 gorilla individuals of two species and identified alleles that encode 8 unique CD4 protein variants.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data analysis from the Great Ape Genome Project as described in the methods and results.

claim: Gorilla CD4 variants show variant-specific differences in susceptibility to virus entry.
source: Functional testing of these identified variant-specific differences in susceptibility to virus entry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, where different gorilla CD4 variants were tested for viral entry.

claim: Single-point mutations from resistant gorilla CD4 variants into permissive human CD4 receptor convey resistance to virus entry.
source: By engineering single-point mutations from resistant gorilla CD4 variants into the permissive human CD4 receptor, we demonstrate that acquired substitutions in gorilla CD4 did convey resistance to virus entry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5, where mutant human CD4s were tested for viral entry.

claim: Selection is acting in favor of more resistant CD4 alleles in ape species harboring SIV endemically (gorillas and chimpanzees), but not in other ape species lacking SIV infections (bonobos and orangutans).
source: We provide a population genetic analysis to support the theory that selection is acting in favor of more and more resistant CD4 alleles in ape species harboring SIV endemically (gorillas and chimpanzees), but not in other ape species that lack SIV infections (bonobos and orangutans).
evidence: This is supported by population genetic analysis shown in Figure 6, comparing CD4 diversity in different ape species.

claim: SIV has placed intense selective pressure on ape CD4, acting to propagate SIV-resistant alleles in chimpanzee and gorilla populations.
source: Taken together, our results show that SIV has placed intense selective pressure on ape CD4, acting to propagate SIV-resistant alleles in chimpanzee and gorilla populations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental and population genetic data presented in the study.

claim: SIVs cause lifelong chronic infections in African monkeys and apes.
source: Simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs) cause lifelong chronic infections in African monkeys and apes (Klatt et al., 2012; Sharp and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SIVs are classified in subfamily Orthoretrovirinae (genus Lentivirus).
source: SIVs are classified in subfamily Orthoretrovirinae (genus Lentivirus) (Coffin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established taxonomic knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Individuals from 45 different African primate species have demonstrated antibodies that react to SIVs in serological tests.
source: Currently, individuals from 45 different African primate species have demonstrated antibodies that react to SIVs in serological tests, and in 37 of these species, SIV exposure has been confirmed by obtaining at least partial sequence of the actual virus (Ayouba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Complete genome sequence is available for only 27 SIVs.
source: Complete genome sequence is available for only 27 SIVs (Ayouba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 90% of tested primate species in Africa have been associated with at least one SIV, indicating nearly pervasive infection of African primates.
source: Remarkably, of the tested primate species in Africa, approximately 90% of them have been associated with at least one SIV, indicating nearly pervasive infection of African primates (Ayouba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SIVcpz arose following cross-species transmission and recombination of multiple SIVs from infected monkeys upon which chimpanzees predate.
source: First, SIV of chimpanzees (SIVcpz) arose following the cross-species transmission and recombination of multiple SIVs from infected monkeys upon which chimpanzees predate (Bailes et al., 2003; Sharp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SIVcpz transmitted to gorillas, giving rise to SIVgor.
source: Subsequently, SIVcpz transmitted to gorillas (giving rise to SIVgor) (Van Heuverswyn et al., 2006; Takehisa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chimpanzees and gorillas have been endemically infected with SIVcpz and SIVgor since those spillover events.
source: Chimpanzees and gorillas have been endemically infected with SIVcpz and SIVgor since those spillover events (Sharp and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Spillover to humans from both chimpanzees and gorillas occurred on multiple occasions.
source: Spillover to humans from both chimpanzees and gorillas subsequently occurred on multiple occasions (Van Heuverswyn et al., 2006; Keele et al., 2006; Plantier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One spillover from apes to humans yielded HIV-1 'group M', the pandemic virus that has infected over 80 million people.
source: One of these spillovers yielded HIV-1 'group M' – the pandemic virus that has swept the globe, infecting over 80 million people.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HIV-1 group M.

claim: Bonobos remain uninfected with SIV.
source: A third great ape species native to Africa, the bonobo, remains uninfected with SIV.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about bonobo SIV infection status.

claim: Orangutans are native to Asia and remain uninfected with SIV.
source: Orangutans, the final great ape species, are native to Asia and also remain uninfected.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about orangutan SIV infection status.

claim: CD4 is the primary entry receptor for primate lentiviruses (SIV and HIV).
source: CD4 is the primary entry receptor for primate lentiviruses (SIV and HIV).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CD4 function.

claim: CD4 is a surface protein expressed on T cells, where it is bound by the viral envelope (Env) glycoprotein to begin viral entry into the cell.
source: CD4 is a surface protein expressed on T cells, where it is bound by the viral envelope (Env) glycoprotein to begin viral entry into the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CD4 function.

claim: CD4 has evolved under positive natural selection over the course of primate evolution.
source: CD4 has evolved under positive natural selection over the course of primate evolution (Meyerson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most of the sequence evolution in CD4 has been concentrated to the region encoding the D1 domain that interacts with HIV and SIV Env.
source: As such, it has been noted that most of the sequence evolution in CD4 has been concentrated to the region encoding the D1 domain that interacts with HIV and SIV Env (Meyerson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different primate orthologs of CD4 vary dramatically in the lentiviruses that they will engage.
source: As a result, we have demonstrated that different primate orthologs of CD4 vary dramatically in the lentiviruses that they will engage (Warren et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge from the authors' previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The reconstructed ancestral CD4 at the hominin node differs from human CD4 by only two nonsynonymous substitutions.
source: The reconstructions of sequences at these ancestral nodes yielded CD4 sequences that differ from human CD4 by only two (hominin) and five (hominid) nonsynonymous substitutions.
evidence: This is supported by the ancestral reconstruction analysis described in the methods and results.

claim: The reconstructed ancestral CD4 at the hominid node differs from human CD4 by five nonsynonymous substitutions.
source: The reconstructions of sequences at these ancestral nodes yielded CD4 sequences that differ from human CD4 by only two (hominin) and five (hominid) nonsynonymous substitutions.
evidence: This is supported by the ancestral reconstruction analysis described in the methods and results.

claim: Only one of the changes between ancestral and human CD4 mapped to the D1 domain of CD4 (N52S).
source: Only one of these changes mapped to the D1 domain of CD4 (N52S; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the ancestral reconstruction analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All tested pseudoviruses displayed similar levels of infection on cells expressing human or the ancestral CD4 proteins.
source: All tested pseudoviruses displayed similar levels of infection on cells expressing human or the ancestral CD4 proteins (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Cells bearing chimpanzee and gorilla CD4s were generally less permissive to virus entry than cells with human or ancestral CD4s.
source: On the other hand, cells bearing chimpanzee and gorilla CD4s were generally less permissive to virus entry (green in Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Selective pressures exerted by SIVs in the chimpanzee and gorilla lineages led to the retention of mutations that now confer resistance to primate lentivirus infection.
source: We conclude that CD4 was originally permissive to primate lentiviruses, but that selective pressures exerted by SIVs in the chimpanzee and gorilla lineages led to the retention of mutations that now confer resistance to primate lentivirus infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing ancestral and modern CD4s.

claim: Multiple CD4 alleles circulate in chimpanzee populations, which encode CD4 variants more resistant to SIVcpz entry than human CD4.
source: We and others have shown that multiple CD4 alleles circulate in chimpanzee populations, which encode CD4 variants more resistant to SIVcpz entry than human CD4 (Bibollet-Ruche et al., 2019; Warren et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Six nonsynonymous and five synonymous SNPs separate the individual CD4 alleles in the gorilla population analyzed.
source: We analyzed genetic data from 32 gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla [n = 28]; Gorilla gorilla diehli [n = 1]; Gorilla beringei graueri [n = 3]) and found six nonsynonymous and five synonymous SNPs separating the individual alleles encoded.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data analysis from the Great Ape Genome Project.

claim: Five out of six of the nonsynonymous polymorphisms in gorilla CD4 are located within the domain 1-encoding region.
source: Five out of six of the nonsynonymous polymorphisms are located within the domain 1-encoding region of CD4 (two are in the same codon, codon 27) and one in domain 2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A study of over 100 fecal samples from gorillas at field sites in Africa identified the same set of SNPs as found in this study.
source: A study of over 100 fecal samples from gorillas at field sites in Africa recently identified the same set of SNPs (Russell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as corroborating evidence from another study, supported by citation.

claim: Gorilla CD4 allele 5 is the most common allele in the population analyzed.
source: The frequencies of these eight alleles are heterogeneous, where allele 5 is the most common (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by frequency data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A predicted N-glycosylation site at position 15 is fixed in the gorilla population but absent in other African apes.
source: From looking at the sequences of these different alleles, we noticed a predicted glycosylation site (N-glycosylation tripeptide NXT) at position 15 that is fixed in the gorilla population but absent in the other African apes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gorilla CD4 allele 2 codes for a proline at position 18, which strongly reduces the likelihood of glycosylation at position 15.
source: Interestingly, the gorilla CD4 allele 2 codes for a proline at position 18, immediately after the tripeptide NCT, which strongly reduces the likelihood of glycosylation (Gavel and von Heijne, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and cited knowledge about glycosylation motifs.

claim: All gorilla CD4 variants were equal to, or more resistant to infection than, human CD4.
source: All gorilla CD4 variants were equal to, or more resistant to infection than, the human CD4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There are considerable differences in the entry phenotype for each SIVcpz strain evaluated, where a single host CD4 variant can be highly restrictive to one strain while being fully functional for entry of another.
source: As such, we found considerable differences on the entry phenotype for each SIVcpz strain evaluated, where a single host CD4 variant can be highly restrictive to one strain, while being fully functional for entry of another.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: SIVcpz TAN2.69 showed a uniformly strong ability to use any of the gorilla CD4 variants.
source: As an outlier, SIVcpz TAN2.69 showed a uniformly strong ability to use any of the gorilla CD4 variants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gorilla variant 3 CD4 supported less entry by SIVcpz TAN1.910 than variant 2 due to the change in glycosylation status.
source: Variant 3, which differs from variant 2 only by this proline, supported less entry by SIVcpz TAN1.910 due to this change in glycosylation status (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human CD4 with the gorilla-specific glycosylation motif at position 15 showed decreased susceptibility to entry compared to wild-type human CD4.
source: We then challenged these cells with pseudoviruses displaying the envelope of different SIVcpz strains and consistently found a decrease in susceptibility to entry compared to wild-type human CD4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Human T15N CD4 and gorilla variant 3 migrated at a higher molecular weight compared to human wild-type CD4 and gorilla variant 2, corresponding to the predicted number of glycans on CD4 domain 1.
source: As expected, human T15N CD4, as well as gorilla variant 3, migrated at a higher molecular weight compared to human wild-type CD4 and gorilla variant 2, corresponding to the predicted number of glycans on CD4 domain 1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with PNGase F caused all CD4 variants to migrate to the same molecular weight, confirming that the mobility shift is due to the glycosylation status of CD4.
source: We then treated the lysates with PNGase F, an N-linked glycosidase, and found that all CD4 variants migrated to the same molecular weight, confirming that the mobility shift is due to the glycosylation status of CD4.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Most gorilla CD4 variants have gained a glycan at position 15 that reduces entry of SIV as compared to human CD4.
source: Thus, most gorilla CD4 variants have gained a glycan at position 15 that reduces entry of SIV as compared to human CD4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on glycosylation and viral entry.

claim: Gorilla CD4 allele 2, which does not encode the glycan at position 15, would be at a fitness disadvantage.
source: It seems that the gorilla CD4 allele 2, which does not encode this glycan, would be at a fitness disadvantage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional data and the low frequency of allele 2.

claim: Allele 2 is one of the least frequent alleles in the gorilla population surveyed.
source: In support of this, allele 2 is one of the least frequent alleles in the gorilla population that we surveyed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by frequency data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutant forms of human CD4 encoding gorilla-specific residues at positions 27, 31, and 34 were significantly more restrictive to at least two of the four SIVcpz strains tested compared to human wild-type CD4.
source: We found that in all cases the mutant form of human CD4 encoding the gorilla-specific amino acid was significantly more restrictive to at least two of the four SIVcpz strains when compared to human wild-type CD4 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: H27R mutation in human CD4 drastically reduced infection by SIVcpz MB897, rendering a fully supportive receptor highly refractory to infection.
source: In several cases, such as H27R CD4 expressing cells infected with SIVcpz MB897, we found drastic effects where a fully supportive receptor was rendered highly refractory to infection by a single amino acid substitution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The protective role of gorilla-specific substitutions in CD4 was SIVcpz strain specific.
source: We found that the protective role of these gorilla-specific substitutions was SIVcpz strain specific, demonstrating that collectively, the diversity found in gorilla individuals can confer relative protection to all the SIV strains we tested, but that SIVs are counter-evolving as well.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing variable effects across different SIV strains.

claim: Single amino acid changes in domain 1 can drastically modify the interaction between CD4 and the lentivirus envelope, directly influencing virus entry.
source: These results suggest that single amino acid changes in domain 1 can drastically modify the interaction between CD4 and the lentivirus envelope, directly influencing virus entry.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on single-point mutations.

claim: Mutating gorilla CD4 to recapitulate human CD4 amino acids did not result in full restoration of entry phenotype, showing only minimal increases in entry of SIVcpz.
source: We did not observe a full restoration of entry phenotype here and instead found only minimal increases in entry of SIVcpz through these receptors (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The resistance to SIVcpz found in gorilla individuals is not dependent on single amino acids, but rather the cumulative effect of multiple amino acid changes.
source: These results imply that the resistance to SIVcpz found in gorilla individuals is not dependent on single amino acids, but rather the cumulative effect of multiple amino acid changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing incomplete restoration of phenotype with single mutations.

claim: Population-level sequence diversity in CD4 of gorillas confers some level of protection against multiple SIVcpz strains.
source: Overall, our data suggest that population-level sequence diversity in CD4 of gorillas confers some level of protection against multiple SIVcpz strains.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental data on gorilla CD4 variants.

claim: Within endemically infected species, nonsynonymous SNPs in CD4 are at a significantly higher frequency compared to neighboring loci.
source: However, within the endemically infected species, nonsynonymous SNPs in CD4 are at a significantly higher frequency compared to neighboring loci, represented by 𝜭π (Figure 6A; Tajima, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by population genetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The difference in nonsynonymous SNP frequency is not observed for synonymous variation in CD4.
source: This difference is not observed for synonymous variation.
evidence: This is supported by population genetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The discordance between nonsynonymous and synonymous variation suggests that the higher frequency of nonsynonymous variants at CD4 in endemically infected species is not explained by neutral or demographic evolutionary forces.
source: This discordance between nonsynonymous and synonymous variation suggests that the higher frequency of nonsynonymous variants at CD4 in the endemically infected species is not explained by neutral or demographic evolutionary forces.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the population genetic analysis.

claim: The higher frequency of segregating nonsynonymous variation is restricted to the endemically infected species.
source: In addition, the higher frequency of segregating nonsynonymous variation is restricted to the endemically infected species.
evidence: This is supported by population genetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: These patterns are consistent with positive selection increasing the frequency of and/or maintaining nonsynonymous SNPs in CD4 within the endemically infected species only.
source: Taken together, these patterns are consistent with positive selection increasing the frequency of and/or maintaining nonsynonymous SNPs in CD4 within the endemically infected species only.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the population genetic analysis.

claim: Gorilla and chimpanzee nonsynonymous polymorphic sites are significantly concentrated on the domain 1 of CD4 when compared to the un/recently infected species.
source: Also, in support of this, we find that gorilla and chimpanzee nonsynonymous polymorphic sites are significantly concentrated on the domain 1 of CD4 when compared to the un/recently infected species (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by population genetic analysis shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Long-term SIV infection in ape populations may be driving nonsynonymous SNPs to higher frequency in CD4, particularly in the region corresponding to domain 1 that directly interacts with the virus Env glycoprotein.
source: These data suggest that long-term SIV infection in ape populations may be driving nonsynonymous SNPs to higher frequency in CD4, particularly in the region corresponding to domain 1 that directly interacts with the virus Env glycoprotein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the population genetic analysis.

claim: CD4 has evolved under strong positive selection throughout the evolution and speciation of simian primates.
source: We and others have previously shown that the CD4 gene has evolved under strong positive selection throughout the evolution and speciation of simian primates (Meyerson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Selection on CD4 is thought to be driven by the direct interaction between CD4 and the HIV/SIV envelope glycoprotein.
source: Selection on CD4 is thought to be driven by the direct interaction between CD4 and the HIV/SIV envelope glycoprotein.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Removing the D1 sequence from the analysis renders the CD4 gene no longer under positive selection.
source: We found that removing the D1 sequence from the analysis renders the gene no longer under positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by the updated positive selection analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most African primate species currently harbor lentiviruses endemically, despite CD4 evolution, meaning that CD4 remains functional for viral entry of at least some viruses.
source: It is important to note that most African primate species currently harbor lentiviruses endemically, despite CD4 evolution, meaning that CD4 remains functional for viral entry of at least some viruses despite the selective pressure to resist it.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about African primate SIV infections.

claim: CD4 is evolving to convey natural tolerance in primates.
source: Therefore, we understand CD4 to be evolving to convey natural tolerance in primates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that CD4 evolves resistance but viruses persist.

claim: Protective glycosylation of CD4 has been observed in chimpanzees.
source: Protective (to the host) glycosylation of CD4 has recently also been observed by us and others in chimpanzees (Bibollet-Ruche et al., 2019; Warren et al., 2019b), and in another population sample of gorillas (Russell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The evolutionary acquisition of a glycan shield on CD4 may be a recurring theme in the evolution of primate species that are plagued with SIVs.
source: Indeed, the evolutionary acquisition of a glycan shield on CD4 may be a recurring theme in the evolution of primate species that are plagued with SIVs (Russell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation based on observations across multiple primate species, supported by citation.

claim: The sequence diversity (within species) and divergence (between species) of several primate genes have been driven by infection pressure from lentiviruses.
source: Collectively, it is now clear that the sequence diversity (within species) and divergence (between species) of several primate genes have been driven by infection pressure from lentiviruses (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Demogines et al., 2010; Han et al., 2011; Johnson and Sawyer, 2009; Judd et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2012; Malfavon-Borja et al., 2013; Meyerson et al., 2018; Meyerson et al., 2015; Meyerson et al., 2014; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2007; Sawyer et al., 2006; Sawyer et al., 2005; Sawyer et al., 2004; Sawyer and Elde, 2012; Stabell et al., 2016; Warren et al., 2024; Warren and Sawyer, 2019c; White et al., 2014; Wilke and Sawyer, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from extensive prior work, supported by multiple citations.

claim: When host genes like CD4 become highly diverse within species, a given virus strain may only be able to infect a small number of individuals within the population.
source: When host genes like CD4 become highly diverse within species, a given virus strain may only be able to infect a small number of individuals within the population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional data on CD4 variants.

claim: Gorilla CD4 variant 1 is highly resistant to most of the SIVs tested.
source: For instance, gorilla CD4 variant 1 is highly resistant to most of the SIVs we tested (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only one SIV isolate, SIVcpz 'TAN2.69', could enter cells through the receptor encoded by gorilla CD4 allele 1.
source: In fact, we only found one SIV isolate, SIVcpz 'TAN2.69', which could enter cells through the receptor encoded by allele 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gorillas homozygous for allele 1 would largely be protected from most circulating SIV strains.
source: This suggests that gorillas homozygous for allele 1 would largely be protected from most circulating SIV strains.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional data for allele 1.

claim: If allele 1 were to become fixed within gorilla populations, many strains of SIV in gorillas could go extinct.
source: Taking this example further, if allele 1 were to become fixed within gorilla populations, many strains of SIV in gorillas could go extinct.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional data for allele 1.

claim: Virus-driven evolution of genes like CD4 means that virus spillover between species, including zoonotic spillovers that yield new human viruses, are less likely to happen.
source: In the long-term, the virus-driven evolution of genes like CD4 also means that virus spillover between species – including the zoonotic spillovers that yield new human viruses – are less likely to happen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the understanding of CD4 evolution and its effects on viral tropism.

claim: Receptor sequence divergence serves as a potent barrier to the movement of viruses between species.
source: Indeed, a prevailing theme that has emerged in recent years is that receptor sequence divergence serves as a potent barrier to the movement of viruses between species (Barbachano-Guerrero et al., 2023; Demogines et al., 2012b; Demogines et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2022; Kaelber et al., 2012; Kerr et al., 2015; Makin, 2022; Meyerson et al., 2014; Nahabedian et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2015; Sawyer and Elde, 2012; Warren et al., 2022; Warren and Sawyer, 2023; Warren and Sawyer, 2019c).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from extensive prior work, supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD4 and RanBP2 played key roles in the transmission of SIVs to apes.
source: Specifically, CD4 and another host protein RanBP2 (Meyerson et al., 2018) played key roles in the transmission of SIVs to apes (see also Sauter and Kirchhoff, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Spillover of lentiviruses between species will only happen when virus is transmitted between key individuals of two different species, where the donor has CD4 alleles yielding high titers and the recipient has CD4 alleles making it receptive to infection.
source: Therefore, spillover of lentiviruses between species will only happen when virus is transmitted between key individuals of two different species. The donor individual would need to have CD4 alleles that yield high titers of SIV in its body, and the recipient individual would need to have CD4 alleles that make it receptive to infection by this new virus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the understanding of CD4 diversity and its effects on viral tropism.
